papers.title: A Study on the Impact of PBL Learning Experience on Entrepreneurial Opportunity Competencies: Focusing on the Moderating Effect of Learning Satisfaction
papers.abstract: With the advent of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, universities are placing greater emphasis on nurturing talents equipped with creativity and problem-solving skills, which is especially critical in entrepreneurship education. Traditional lecture-based teaching methods are being replaced by more active learning approaches where students engage in solving real-world problems. In this context, Problem-Based Learning (PBL) has emerged as an effective instructional strategy for enhancing entrepreneurial opportunity recognition competency. Entrepreneurial opportunity competency refers to an individual's ability to identify opportunities in the environment and transform them into feasible business ideas. As youth entrepreneurship becomes a national strategic priority, strengthening this competency among university students is not only important for individual career development but also for enhancing national competitiveness. This study aims to empirically examine the impact of PBL participation on university students’ entrepreneurial opportunity competency and to investigate whether learning satisfaction moderates this relationship. A survey was conducted from November 1 to December 20, 2024, targeting students enrolled in four-year universities in Gyeonggi Province who had participated in PBL-based courses. A total of 140 valid responses were analyzed. The findings indicate, first, that students’ ability to identify and solve problems through PBL positively influences their entrepreneurial opportunity competency. This suggests that the process of experimenting with diverse problem-solving strategies and accumulating experience during PBL enhances essential entrepreneurial skills. It highlights the need for universities to actively adopt PBL-based curricula and develop a variety of problem-centered educational programs. Second, the moderating effect of learning satisfaction was confirmed: the positive impact of PBL participation on entrepreneurial opportunity competency was stronger among students with higher satisfaction levels. This implies that when learners are more satisfied with the learning process, their sense of achievement and motivation in problem-solving is heightened, thereby further enhancing their entrepreneurial competencies.

papers.title: Enhancing Kindergarten Letter Recognition Through Play-Based Learning
papers.abstract: CABALLO, J.T.T., CASTOR, H.A., LAZATIN, H.M., and TABAFA, L.J., Central Mindanao University, Musuan, Maramag, Bukidnon, Enhancing Kindergarten Letter Recognition Through Play-Based Learning. Adviser: Gladys S. Escarlos, PhD This study investigated the effectiveness of a play-based learning intervention, the Letter Jump Game, in enhancing letter recognition skills among kindergarten learners at Musuan Integrated School. The research aimed to address the limitations of traditional instructional strategies in early literacy by introducing an interactive and developmentally appropriate approach tailored to young learners. Specifically, it sought to determine whether the integration of kinesthetic movement and cognitive engagement through play could improve learners’ ability to recognize uppercase and lowercase letters. A quasi-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design was employed. Fifteen purposively selected kindergarten pupils aged 4 to 6 years old participated in the study. Pre-test and post-test assessments measured their letter recognition levels before and after a three-week intervention period, during which the Letter Jump Game was implemented three times per week. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and paired samples t-tests. Results showed an increase in mean scoresfrom 12.33 to 14.47 for lowercase letters and 14.20 to 15.47 for uppercase letters, indicating improved recognition skills. However, these improvements were not statistically significant (p > 0.05). Despite this, qualitative observations noted increased engagement, confidence, and participation, especially among kinesthetic learners and those who initially struggled. The study concludes that while the intervention did not yield statistically significant results, it demonstrated practical benefits in promoting early literacy skills through active learning. The findings support the integration of play-based and kinesthetic strategies into early childhood instruction and recommend further research with larger samples and extended durations to validate the approach’s effectiveness.
